title: NVlabs/ASPIRE — ASPIRE: Agentic /Skills Discovery for Robotics
content:
ASPIRE is a new type of continual learning: "training" is skill refinement instead of gradient descent.
"Trained model" is a repo of sensorimotor skills instead of floating weights.
“Distributed training” is a panel of agents each practicing a different skill instead of sharded minibatches.
- [2026-10] ASPIRE v1.0 is out! ASPIRE can now solve a Rubik's Cube, and it achieves 99% success on 80 LIBERO-Pro Goal / Object / Spatial / Long tasks and selected Robosuite, BEHAVIOR-1K tasks.
- [2026-06] ASPIRE is out! We achieve SOTA results on LIBERO-Pro, Robosuite, and BEHAVIOR-1K with Claude Opus 4.6! Also check out our table bussing sim-to-real demos!
ASPIRE improves with the underlying model. On 10 LIBERO-Pro tasks, success rises from 15% (GPT-6 Luna) to 99% (Claude Opus 5.5), and the strongest models are not the most expensive: the green line marks the cost/success frontier. Across LIBERO-Pro, Robosuite and BEHAVIOR-1K, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches 97–100% success on every task.
To get started with ASPIRE, launch a coding agent such as Codex or Claude Code and enter the following prompt:
Clone the main branch of https://github.com/NVlabs/ASPIRE/,
read the iterative-debugging skill (.claude/skills/iterative-debugging/SKILL.md) and
docs/libero-pro.md, and run the complete ASPIRE LIBERO-Pro Goal-Swap Quick Start for
all ten tasks in the libero_goal_swap suite.
Before executing, report the required GPUs, credentials, gated weights,
services, expected runtime, seed partitions, and output paths. Wait for
my confirmation before launching. Do not access real-robot code or instructions
(AGENTS.md, docs/system2*.md, docs/yam-real.md, src/cap_harness/yam_real/).
Before running, set up the host (CUDA, uv, and the Hugging Face token for the gated SAM3 weights) with docs/host-setup.md.
Reference agent environments: ASPIRE is coding-agent agnostic. The simulation workflow is packaged as agent skills for Claude Code (.claude/skills/) and Codex (.codex/skills/): iterative-debugging and evosearch. AGENTS.md holds the execution rules for the real-robot System 2 agent (operator runbook) and is not needed for simulation runs.
Name the suite and experiment explicitly. If neither is named, the agent should present this table and stop for selection.
Before a paper-scale launch, the agent must report the selected tasks, seed schedule, expected trial count and runtime, GPU and credential requirements, services, and output paths, then wait for explicit confirmation.
Use the System 2 operator runbook to prepare a calibrated YAM station and launch a fresh agent with the appropriate text-based task skill:
The manipulation skill entrypoint routes the agent to these recipes. They provide grasp strategies, recovery, and physical completion checks without requiring episode logs or fixed-coordinate replays. The three new recipes are distilled from demo sessions, not a new real-robot validation; the pill recipe explicitly distinguishes a seated cap from verified final tightness. Re-ground the current scene and verify the actual outcome.
Warning
ASPIRE executes language-model-generated Python with full import access. Trial processes and watchdogs are not a security sandbox. Run generated code on an isolated host without credentials or sensitive mounts, restrict network access, and never grant a simulation agent access to physical hardware. Real-robot work requires the controls in aspire/real/AGENTS.md and separate operator authorization.
Start with CONTRIBUTING.md. Third-party contributions must include a Developer Certificate of Origin sign-off.
ASPIRE material owned by NVIDIA or contributed under the project license is available under the Apache License 2.0. Third-party materials retain their original terms. See NOTICE and the central licensing and compliance index before using or redistributing the full stack.
If you find ASPIRE useful in your research, please cite:
@article{lu2026aspire,
  title   = {ASPIRE: Agentic /Skills Discovery for Robotics},
  author  = {Runyu Lu and Yubo Wu and Ethan Kou and Haotian Lin and Letian Fu and Wenli Xiao and
             Ajay Mandlekar and Yinzhen Xu and Guanya Shi and Ken Goldberg and
             Ang Chen and Mosharaf Chowdhury and Jan Kautz and Yuke Zhu and Linxi "Jim" Fan and Guanzhi Wang},
  year    = {2026},
  journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2607.00272},
  url     = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00272}
}
ASPIRE was developed by researchers from NVIDIA, the University of Michigan, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, UC Berkeley, and Carnegie Mellon University.

report.summary: NVIDIA-led ASPIRE replaces gradient-descent training with agent-discovered, reusable sensorimotor skills, reporting near-100% success on several robot manipulation benchmarks.
report.background: Robot learning has largely converged on end-to-end policies trained by gradient descent, but every new task or embodiment forces another fine-tuning cycle, and the resulting weights are opaque, brittle and hard to audit. A parallel line of work — Code as Policies, SayCan, VoxPoser — argued that pretrained language and vision models can instead write reusable programs that call perception and motion primitives, letting the model, not the optimizer, do the generalizing. ASPIRE sits at the intersection of that idea and the rise of agentic coding assistants: if a coding agent can iteratively debug a repository, it can also iteratively debug a robot skill until the simulator reports success. The output is a skill library that improves as base models improve. NVIDIA researchers led the project with collaborators from Michigan, UIUC, Berkeley and CMU; some reported model names and 2026 milestones read as forward-looking projections.
key_points: ASPIRE redefines the vocabulary of machine learning. "Training" becomes skill refinement rather than gradient descent; the "trained model" is a repository of sensorimotor skills rather than floating weights; "distributed training" is a panel of agents each practicing a different skill rather than sharded minibatches. Capability is therefore stored as readable, editable code and recipes instead of a weight matrix.

Performance tracks the underlying foundation model closely. On ten LIBERO-Pro tasks, success climbs from 15% with GPT-6 Luna to 99% with Claude Opus 5.5, and the project reports a cost/success frontier showing the strongest models are not the most expensive. Across LIBERO-Pro, Robosuite and BEHAVIOR-1K, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches 97–100%. Version 1.0 adds Rubik's Cube solving and 99% on 80 LIBERO-Pro tasks.

The workflow is packaged for coding agents and is agent-agnostic. Simulation skills ship in .claude/skills and .codex/skills, including iterative-debugging and evosearch loops, so a single prompt can clone the repo, read the docs and launch a benchmark. Human gates are built in: the agent must first report GPUs, credentials, gated weights, services, runtime, seeds and output paths, then wait for confirmation.

A real-robot path exists but is deliberately fenced off. A System 2 operator runbook prepares a calibrated YAM station, and manipulation recipes supply grasp strategies, recovery and physical completion checks without episode logs or fixed-coordinate replays. The authors caution the recipes are distilled from demos, not fresh validation — the pill task distinguishes a seated cap from verified tightness.

Safety and licensing are stated bluntly. ASPIRE executes model-generated Python with full import access, and trial watchdogs are explicitly not a sandbox; users are told to isolate hosts, restrict network access and never give a simulation agent hardware access. Code is Apache 2.0 with a DCO requirement for contributions and a NOTICE file covering third-party terms.
report.impact: For the AI industry, ASPIRE reframes robotics progress as a software-engineering problem: capability tracks the quality of coding agents and the skill library, not the size of a policy network. That shifts value toward harnesses, evaluation suites and reusable skill repositories. For developers, the barrier drops sharply — a prompt plus an isolated GPU host can reproduce a benchmark, and the released skill folders offer a template for packaging any robotics workflow as agent-readable instructions. For regular users, the promise is cheaper, more legible automation: failures trace to a named skill file rather than a weight matrix, and cost/success frontiers suggest mid-tier models may suffice. The caveats matter: results are simulation-heavy, real-robot recipes remain lightly validated, and executing model-written Python demands strict isolation.
report.tools: Start at github.com/NVlabs/ASPIRE and read CONTRIBUTING.md; drive it with Claude Code or Codex, whose .claude/skills and .codex/skills folders hold the iterative-debugging and evosearch loops. Benchmarks to watch: LIBERO-Pro, Robosuite, BEHAVIOR-1K. Expect CUDA, uv, and a Hugging Face token for gated SAM3 weights. For conceptual grounding, read Code as Policies, SayCan and VoxPoser — and run everything on an isolated host.
